## The idea

Add one more stacked third to a triad and the chord gains another internal line.
C-E-G-B sounds spacious and unsettled in a different way from C-E-G-B-flat.
Both contain a major triad, but their sevenths point in different directions.

A *seventh chord* has four tones built in thirds. Major seventh, minor seventh,
dominant seventh, and half-diminished seventh each have a distinct interval
array. The dominant seventh is the useful pressure point: G-B-D-F contains B-F,
a tritone whose two notes sit one semitone outside C and E.

## Run this

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 76
use_synth :piano

qualities = {
  major_7: [0, 4, 7, 11],
  minor_7: [0, 3, 7, 10],
  dominant_7: [0, 4, 7, 10],
  half_diminished_7: [0, 3, 6, 10]
}

qualities.each do |name, offsets|
  notes = offsets.map { |offset| note(:c4) + offset }
  puts name
  play_chord notes, release: 1.7
  sleep 2
  notes.each { |pitch| play pitch, release: 0.35; sleep 0.4 }
  sleep 1
end

dominant = [55, 59, 62, 65]
tonic = [55, 60, 64, 67]

define :play_resolution do |from, to, solo|
  voices = solo.nil? ? (0...from.length).to_a : [solo]
  voices.each do |index|
    in_thread do
      play from[index], release: 1.4, amp: 0.7
      sleep 2
      play to[index], release: 1.8, amp: 0.7
    end
  end
  sleep 4
end

play_resolution dominant, tonic, nil
4.times { |voice| play_resolution dominant, tonic, voice }
```

The first section gives every quality as a block and then exposes its tones.
The resolution follows G7 to C one line at a time. B rises to C while F falls to
E. Those contrary semitone motions are the centre of the cadence.

## Change one thing

1. Remove F from `dominant`. The remaining G major triad still points to C, but
   the tritone and its downward resolution disappear.
2. Resolve F upward to G instead of downward to E. The chord reaches C with a
   suspended tone, delaying one part of the arrival.
3. Lower B to B-flat. The tritone changes and the chord no longer acts as the
   ordinary dominant of C major.

## Why it works

Seventh-chord quality is an offset set relative to a root. Major 7 and dominant
7 differ only at the top note. Minor 7 lowers both third and seventh.
Half-diminished 7 also lowers the fifth. Block labels hide these local changes;
the arrays show them.

Within G7, B and F span six semitones. Each lies one semitone from a stable tone
in C major. Resolving B upward and F downward contracts the tritone into a major
third. G can stay as a common tone, while D may move to C or E. Four simultaneous
melodies produce what the ear groups as one harmonic event.

The `solo` argument is a debugging switch. It isolates one indexed line without
changing the score data. This is useful whenever a dense chord masks the motion
that explains its effect.

Root choice changes function as well as colour. C dominant seventh contains
C-E-G-B-flat and points most readily toward F, while C major seventh contains B
and can sit as a tonic colour in C major. One offset controls that distinction.
The shared lower triad is therefore insufficient to name the chord's job. Hear
the seventh before treating `major_7` and `dominant_7` as nearby dictionary keys.

Doubling introduces another decision. The four-note arrays state each chord tone
once, but a four-voice resolution may double the tonic and omit the fifth. That
is a voicing policy applied after chord construction. Keeping those layers apart
lets the same dominant-seventh record feed a keyboard block, an arpeggio, or four
independent lines.

## Take it further

Add inversions of G7 and C to the candidate set from Lesson 27. Search for a
resolution where B moves to C, F moves to E, no voice leaps more than five
semitones, and voices never cross. Print the chosen pairs and total movement,
then play the full resolution followed by each line alone.
